status_summary: USAID no longer exists, so the outcome is judged in State, Treasury and the wider executive branch, where the cessation elements of the text are operative but affirmative support for oil and gas in aid programs was not found. Executive Order 14162 (signed 2025-01-20) revoked the US International Climate Finance Plan, ended UNFCCC financial commitments and set economic efficiency and American prosperity as priorities for foreign energy engagement, and a memorandum of 2026-01-07 directed withdrawal from bodies including the UNFCCC, the IPCC and the International Renewable Energy Agency, ceasing funding to the extent permitted by law. The EXIM board, an export credit agency rather than an aid agency, approved a loan of nearly $5 billion for the Mozambique LNG project on 2025-03-14, and Treasury has urged the World Bank since April 2025, most recently in a statement reported on 2026-10-15, to finance gas and upstream oil and gas projects. The FY2026 appropriations law enacted 2026-02-03 still funds the Global Environment Facility at $150.2 million per CRS, and rescission of the 2021 guidance on overseas fossil fuel financing was not verified, so the record is held at the bottom of the implemented band.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14162 was signed (published 2025-01-30 at 90 FR 8455); Sec. 3(e) revoked the US International Climate Finance Plan, Sec. 3(c) directed ceasing UNFCCC financial commitments, Sec. 3(f) required agency reports on rescinding policies that advanced the plan, and Sec. 3(g) set priorities of economic efficiency and American prosperity for foreign energy engagement.
The US EXIM board approved a loan of nearly $5 billion for the TotalEnergies-led Mozambique LNG project, clearing a hurdle to restart it.

The World Bank board decided to end its ban on financing nuclear energy projects, a change the US had pushed for, without agreeing on upstream gas financing (dated by the report; the decision date is not stated in the source).

A presidential memorandum was signed (published 2026-01-16 at 91 FR 2281) directing withdrawal from 66 international organizations (35 non-UN and 31 UN entities), including the UNFCCC, the IPCC and the International Renewable Energy Agency, with participation in or funding to UN entities to cease to the extent permitted by law.

The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75), including the FY2026 National Security, Department of State and Related Programs act, was enacted; the House Appropriations Committee summary says it eliminates funding for the prior administration's climate executive orders and climate change mandates.

title: Stop opposing fossil fuel development abroad and narrow climate funding in foreign aid
uncertainties: The rescission of the 2021 interim guidance on international public financing of fossil fuel projects and of Treasury's multilateral development bank energy guidance was not confirmed: the researcher's searches and one reviewer search returned only 2021 coverage of the guidance. EO 14162 does not name those documents. The House committee summary prints no date and is dated here to the law's enactment on 2026-02-03; that enactment date was confirmed on 2026-10-26 on the GovInfo slip law header for Public Law 119-75 (H.R. 7148), so it no longer rests on the bill tracker (thelobbynews.com). The summary gives no figures for the climate eliminations, and CRS lists zero FY2026 funding for the Clean Technology Fund and for Tropical Forest and Coral Reef Conservation without explanation. A search for DFC financing of oil or gas projects in 2025 or 2026 returned only older financings. EXIM is an export credit agency, so its LNG loan is a parallel step, not foreign aid. Whether specific climate-advocacy NGOs and foundations lost funding was not separately verified; the withdrawal memorandum covers international bodies only. Mandate text on the Climate Strategy 2022 to 2030 and Paris-related programs is tracked in c09-03. Division F of P.L. 119-75 could not be read: the GovInfo HTML, as retrieved in two reviews, ended within Division A, Title VIII (at Sec. 8072 in one retrieval and Sec. 8042 on 2026-10-26) and did not reach Division F, and no division-level text was found on rules.house.gov, appropriations.senate.gov or congress.gov, so the Global Environment Facility line was confirmed only through the CRS report and any climate-order funding limit only through the House committee summary. An OMB Statement of Administration Policy on the Senate amendment to H.R. 7148 (whitehouse.gov, no date printed) was read on 2026-10-26 and mentions no climate provisions. EO 14162 was read in full on the Federal Register and contains no provision on fossil fuel financing guidance or on funding climate-advocacy organizations. Treasury positions at the multilateral development banks are kept as context rather than timeline events because they are statements, not actions: a speech of 2025-04-23 urging the World Bank to move away from climate finance targets, a US statement to the IMF policy committee in April 2025 (dated 2025-04-25 from its meeting dates) calling for an all-of-the-above energy approach including gas, and a statement to the World Bank and IMF steering committees reported on 2026-10-15 asking the Bank to end its ban on upstream oil and gas financing, with no Bank response reported. The CRS report of 2026-07-15 is likewise kept as the source for the Global Environment Facility figure rather than as an event. The 2025-06-12 entry is a World Bank board action, dated by the news report, that the US had pressed for. The rescission of the 2021 interim guidance and of Treasury's multilateral development bank energy guidance was searched again on 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-26 and still not confirmed, and a search for DFC oil and gas financing returned only older financings.
